A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MemeSense framework and datasets. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original intervention-generation experiments, ablations, error analyses, and human-evaluation correlations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds coefficient ablations, representation analyses, runtime measurements, and annotation-agreement results.

M1.justification: The three-stage procedure, exemplar-retrieval strategies, learned per-layer cognitive shift vectors and coefficients, and combined training objective remain unchanged. Expanded demonstration counts concern experimental configurations; fixing the coefficient is an ablation, not a replacement method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 484 curated harmful memes, the same 15 commonsense categories, and 985 usable ICMM examples. Textual and non-textual meme coverage remains unchanged. New diagnostic analyses and category illustrations do not establish additional datasets or task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2–4 retain direct prompting, commonsense-enhanced prompting, random/image/commonsense-anchored ICL, MemeGuard, and MemeMQA. MemeQA and MemeMQA refer to the same adapted comparator. The new runtime comparison uses existing prompting approaches at different shot counts.

E3.justification: Section 6 expands demonstration counts from {1,2,4} to {1,2,4,8,10} and combined-retrieval c from {1,2} to {1,2,4}. New evaluation protocols include fixing alpha to one, comparing first-token representations from five-meme samples and co-occurring categories, and measuring ICMM runtime including training costs. These extend evaluation design without establishing that the unchanged benchmark tables were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds an ablation testing learned coefficients, two analyses of representation structure, runtime analysis, and an Appendix C case study examining partial versus misleading commonsense inputs. Random-commonsense sensitivity, intervention-quality assessment, and alternative-backbone results already existed in v1's appendices and are relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 introduces Mann–Whitney U significance testing against MemeGuard and MemeMQA across Tables 2–4, marking results at p < 0.05. It also first reports Cohen's kappa for harmfulness annotation. The earlier human-rating correlations are retained; no increase in repeated runs or seeds is reported.

E6.justification: Matched benchmark scores and previous appendix results remain unchanged, but substantial diagnostic results are added. Table 6 reports SeSS of 0.61/0.66/0.21 with fixed coefficients versus 0.71/0.78/0.31 for the full model. Table 10 reports 111.5 minutes for MemeSense training plus inference versus 160.8 minutes for four-shot ICL. New representation results include distances of 0.21 versus 0.28 and correlation −0.67; annotation kappa is 0.82.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and four method equations are substantively unchanged. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs. The added representation analyses are empirical rather than new mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: The framework, dataset, and performance-superiority contributions remain. v2 adds an explicit 'up to 35% higher semantic similarity' headline claim in the abstract and baseline-specific gain claims in Section 7. These reframe retained benchmark numbers rather than demonstrate a new capability; the introduction's earlier percentage and near-doubling claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning adaptive coefficient regulation, semantic structure in representations, resilience to partially correct commonsense, and training-versus-inference cost. Appendix B also explains the dataset's sexual-content skew. Conversely, v1's specific limitations concerning adversarial inputs, linguistic nuances, and emerging harmful categories disappear, while its detailed ethical discussion is condensed into a broader-impact statement.

D1.justification: v2 identifies RoBERTa-large and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 as metric backbones, expands annotation guidance, reports 18 corrections among 484 memes, and supplies runtime information. It omits v1's explicit 40% review-sampling detail and code/data access link. Core training hyperparameters and prompt contents remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chen et al. (2025), Qin et al. (2024), and Huang et al. (2024) when grounding exemplar selection and task-vector learning, while removing Liu et al. (2024) and Mazhar et al. (2025). The overall positioning remains stable. Publication updates for retained references do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: The abstract, portions of the introduction, and related-work prose are rewritten. Baseline descriptions are consolidated, and existing sensitivity, intervention-quality, and alternative-model analyses move from appendices into Section 8. The appendix organization changes substantially, and separate limitations and ethics sections are replaced by a shorter broader-impact statement.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column format with a predominantly single-column layout, changes typography and table styling, and relocates existing figures and tables. It adds tables for coefficient ablation, runtime, and commonsense-perturbation cases, plus Figure 4 illustrating all 15 categories. The existing framework schematic is retained with an expanded caption.

improvement.justification: The coefficient ablation, runtime comparison, significance tests, and clearer annotation and metric documentation provide useful additional support and transparency. The overall gain is limited: central benchmark evidence remains unchanged, representation analyses are small exploratory studies, and removal of the code/data link and specific limitations weakens reproducibility guidance and qualification of the claims.
